3.1 Sample composition and descriptive statistics


The data for estimating the audit fee model comes from various sources. We use
Audit Analytics to obtain audit fee data for the years from 2000 to 2010. <sup>10</sup> Financial
data is obtained from the Compustat database and matched to the audit fee data. Our
final sample of firm-years for which we can compute UAF is 54,545, which reduces
to 37,461 when we require sufficient data to compute AQ. <sup>11</sup>

Table 1 Panel A presents descriptive statistics for the variables used to estimate
UAF. Panel B presents the results of the regression used to estimate UAF. As
expected, most variables are significant and in the predicted direction. Audit fees are
positively associated with Big 4 auditors, larger firms, more business segments,

9 Section 404 of the Sarbanes–Oxley Act (SOX) requires management to provide an assessment of the
firm’s internal controls in the annual report and auditors are required to provide an opinion on
management’s assessment.

10 The SEC mandated in 2000 that firms disclose audit and non-audit fees paid to their auditors.

11 The estimation of UAF requires a maximum of two years of data, which is a less stringent data
requirement than other accounting quality proxies (e.g., AQ requires seven years of data). However,
because audit fee data is only available beginning in 2000 it is not possible to calculate UAF for years
before 2000.

larger foreign operations, larger inventories, larger receivables, more employees,
presence of mergers, the presence of losses, any non-standard opinion, and higher
litigation risk. We also find that IPO and SEO years have significantly higher audit
fees. Negatively associated with audit fees are higher current ratios, higher book to
market ratios, higher leverage, non-December fiscal year-ends, and higher return on
assets. The explained variance measured using the adjusted R <sup>2</sup> over the 110
estimations by year and size deciles is 85.4 %. <sup>12</sup>

Table 2 provides details on the characteristics of firms with high accounting
quality (lowest UAF quartile) and low accounting quality (highest UAF quartile).
Firms with estimated low quality accounting tend to be larger, both in terms of
assets and sales, than the firms with high quality accounting. Notice that the
directional association with size is the opposite of other measures, such as AQ,
which classifies smaller firms as having lower quality earnings (Francis et al. 2005;
Liu and Wysocki 2007). Profitability, leverage, and book-to-market ratios appear
comparable between the lowest and highest accounting quality quartiles, with both
groups having a median ROA = 1 %, low (high) accounting quality firms having a
median debt to assets of 18 % (16 %), and low (high) accounting quality firms
having book to market ratio of 0.42 (0.45). <sup>13</sup>
